literature.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
literature.what_it_means: Addresses safe deployment of risk-targeting AI and heterogeneous treatment effects—core to Signal. Methods paper with theoretical guarantees and semi-synthetic validation, not real-world deployment evidence yet.

literature.title: DeDiCa: A Scalable Deconfounding Discrete Causal Generative Model
literature.what_it_means: Methodological advance in causal inference with hidden confounding could support Waymark's causal-evaluation interests, but no empirical validation on health or Medicaid data; transferability undemonstrated.

literature.title: Recognizing Study Lineage Is Not Enough: Over-Crediting Same-Trial Evidence in LLM-Based Medical Verification
literature.what_it_means: Directly addresses LLM safety in medical evidence synthesis—core to Anchor's verification layer. But study is purely computational with no patient data, payer, or clinical workflow. Transfer to Medicaid context requires validation on real care decisions.

literature.title: Federated causal inference for effect estimation in healthcare: methods, challenges, and applications
literature.what_it_means: Methods review addresses Waymark's interest in causal evaluation with observational data across distributed settings. But abstract lacks empirical validation in Medicaid managed care; applicability depends on methodological solutions to confounding and heterogeneity.

literature.title: Automated Calculation of the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Intra-Abdominal Injury Rule from Unstructured Emergency Department Notes Using a Large Language Model
literature.venue: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
literature.what_it_means: Demonstrates LLM reliability for extracting structured data from clinical notes—directly relevant to Waymark's Anchor product and NLP methods interest. However, population (pediatric ED trauma) and setting (acute emergency care) differ substantially from Waymark's Medicaid chronic-disease population.

literature.title: Performance Evaluation of the Latest General-Purpose Large Language Models in Medical Reasoning and Clinical Screening Tasks
literature.what_it_means: Paper validates LLM performance on medical reasoning and screening, relevant to Anchor's omission-error detection role. However, orthopedic literature screening does not transfer to Medicaid care-coordination tasks or member outreach.

literature.title: Lessons From a Quality Improvement Initiative to Address Transportation Barriers in an Urban Primary Care Practice
literature.venue: Journal of primary care & community health
literature.what_it_means: Directly addresses unmet social needs (transportation) that Waymark tackles. Workflow integration and rideshare model are plausibly applicable. But n=22 pilot lacks comparison group, causal evidence, or Medicaid-specific validation.

literature.title: Patterns of social determinants of health screening and health-related social needs among patients with newly diagnosed breast cancer in a safety-net system
literature.what_it_means: Documents SDOH screening patterns and reassessment timing in a vulnerable population. Transferable to Medicaid but disease-specific (breast cancer) and descriptive only—no intervention or causal claim tested.

literature.title: Navigating Health Information Sharing to Address Social Needs: Practice, Research, and Policy Recommendations from Hospital-Based Violence Intervention
literature.venue: The Journal of law, medicine & ethics : a journal of the American Society of Law, Medicine & Ethics
literature.what_it_means: Addresses information-sharing barriers relevant to Waymark's social-needs and care-coordination work. However, this is a qualitative policy-practice paper without empirical impact data on outcomes or operations.

literature.title: The Intersection of Place and Need: How Lack of Enrollment Offices Deters Participation in the Safety Net
literature.what_it_means: Addresses structural barriers to safety-net participation using quasi-experimental methods. Relevant to Waymark's re-enrollment (waypoint) and social-needs navigation, but SNAP enrollment differs from Medicaid re-enrollment workflows and member engagement.

literature.title: Hepatitis C screening strategies and linkage-to-care approaches in U.S. emergency departments: A systematic review and meta-analysis
literature.what_it_means: Review compares CHW-led navigation to other linkage strategies for HCV, relevant to Waymark's care-coordination model. However, ED-specific context and outcome focus (HCV cure) differ from Waymark's broader population-health approach. Medicaid fit unclear; payer mix not specified.

literature.title: Automated, Component-Level Assessment of a National Inpatient Diabetes Guideline: Adherence and Its Association with Hospitalization Complications Across Six Hospitals
literature.what_it_means: Inpatient diabetes guideline adherence in Israeli hospitals does not directly transfer to Waymark's outpatient Medicaid population. No Medicaid or US setting. Automation approach and causal methods (IPTW) are methodologically relevant but population/setting mismatch is substantial.

literature.title: Social Needs Z Codes and Subsequent Acute Care Across 21 U.S. Health Systems
literature.what_it_means: Challenges Waymark's assumption that Z codes reliably identify hardship for targeting. Shows documentation varies 1–24% across systems; 46–70% of association is administrative artifact, not hardship signal.

literature.title: Enfermeiro gestor de caso no acompanhamento de utentes crónicos em ambiente hospitalar na transição para a comunidade: scoping review
literature.what_it_means: Scoping review of nurse case management for hospital-to-community transitions in chronic disease. Only 10 studies included, mostly non-US settings. Population and payer context differ from US Medicaid managed care.

literature.title: Community health workers and promotores de salud: a tiered framework for infectious disease prevention and care among California agricultural workers
literature.what_it_means: Directly addresses CHW effectiveness in high-need populations with low healthcare engagement and social barriers. Proposes integrated, tiered CHW model. However, agricultural workers differ from typical Medicaid managed-care populations; Medicaid fit unclear without explicit transfer argument.

literature.title: Improving Continuous Glucose Monitoring Access Among Adults With Type 1 Diabetes in an Urban Safety-Net Hospital
literature.what_it_means: Safety-net setting serves uninsured/Medicaid populations. Pharmacy and care-coordination teams could adopt CGM education and workflow redesign. No explicit Medicaid managed-care context; internal improvement study without external comparison group.

literature.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects of a Prescription for Produce Subsidy on Diabetes Care Management
literature.what_it_means: HTE analysis of food subsidy for diabetes is relevant to Waymark's social-needs navigation and screening. Population is food-insecure with chronic disease. Setting is US primary care but not Medicaid-specific; insurance mix unclear. Effect sizes modest.

literature.title: The Cost of Inaction in Treating Obesity in the U.S
literature.what_it_means: Modeling study projecting obesity treatment benefits across populations including Medicaid. Relevant to whom Waymark reaches (adults with obesity, chronic disease) but provides no operational evidence about care-team interventions, product behavior, or program evaluation methods Waymark uses.

literature.title: AI safety is a system property, not a sum of individual defenses
literature.what_it_means: Waymark deploys LLMs (Compass) in clinical contexts with vulnerable populations. Understanding how safety failures compound—especially jailbreaking affecting hallucination and fairness—directly informs safe product design and evaluation of omission errors.

literature.title: Beyond the black box in healthcare operations: a structured literature review and governance framework for explainable AI in clinical process intelligence systems
literature.what_it_means: Framework addresses XAI governance for operational systems (relevant to Waymark's Signal, Compass, Anchor products), but review is descriptive, not empirical. Framework is preliminary and explicitly lacks external validation.

literature.title: Relationship extraction for adverse drug events in clinical notes using large language models: a retrospective cross-sectional study
literature.what_it_means: NLP for ADE extraction could improve pharmacist safety review (Waymark program), but study lacks Medicaid population, capitated care context, and outcome validation on actionable safety improvement.

literature.title: Federally Qualified Health center–level characteristics associated with sustaining tobacco screening and treatment in the United States, 2020–2024
literature.what_it_means: Identifies FQHC capacity factors predicting sustained screening performance. Relevant to Waymark's care-coordination and outreach design for low-income Medicaid members, but cross-sectional design cannot support causal claims about interventions or care-team actions.

literature.title: Association of Visual Impairment With Medication Adherence and Unintentional Nonadherence Behaviors in Older Adults With Chronic Diseases: A Cross-Sectional Observational Study
literature.venue: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
literature.what_it_means: Identifies a barrier (visual impairment) that pharmacists could screen for and address via simplification, pill organizers, or audio support. Single-center China study with small n limits US Medicaid transferability; cross-sectional design cannot establish causation or treatment effect.

literature.title: Enhancing Scientific Validity by Integrating EHR and Claims Data in the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative
literature.what_it_means: Methodologically relevant to Waymark's causal evaluation interests (target trial emulation), but population is Medicare-only, not Medicaid. Transfer argument needed.

literature.title: Faster but Not Truer, Part 1: A Systematic Scoping Review of Artificial Intelligence in Health Economics and Outcomes Research
literature.venue: Journal of health economics and outcomes research
literature.what_it_means: Directly addresses AI performance measurement gaps and validation failures in causal inference—relevant to Signal and Anchor. But population is HEOR literature, not Medicaid operations. Transferability unclear without Waymark-specific analysis.

literature.title: Real-world evaluation of a multilingual agentic retrieval-augmented clinical AI framework for evidence-grounded medical decision support
literature.what_it_means: Directly relevant to Anchor's error-detection mission and AI safety priorities. However, this is a benchmark study of physician-facing AI tools, not a real-world evaluation of patient outcomes or care-team behavior in Medicaid settings.

literature.title: Human-in-the-loop large language model framework for identification of cutaneous immune-related adverse events
literature.what_it_means: Framework demonstrates LLM safety via human-in-the-loop design and NLP for note analysis. Oncology setting does not directly transfer to Waymark's Medicaid population, but error-detection methods may inform Anchor validation logic.

literature.title: A multi-stage validation framework for trustworthy large-scale clinical information extraction using large language models
literature.what_it_means: Directly addresses LLM safety and omission-error evaluation in clinical-note processing—core to Anchor and Signal. Demonstrates scalable validation without exhaustive annotation, relevant to Waymark's NLP and AI safety interests.

literature.title: Postpartum Maternal Preferences on Health-Related Social Needs Programs in the First 1000 Days
literature.what_it_means: Qualitative study of maternal preferences on social needs screening timing and resource navigation. Findings could inform Waymark's social-needs program design and care-coordination workflows, but evidence is descriptive without quantified program impact or causal inference.

literature.title: Large language models as raters of hospital incident reports: a blinded multi-model evaluation of severity under-grading and shared errors
literature.venue: Joint Commission journal on quality and patient safety
literature.what_it_means: Directly tests LLM safety for clinical classification—relevant to Waymark's Anchor product (AI verification layer). However, study uses hospital incident reports, not Waymark's care-note context. Transfer to Medicaid care coordination requires validation.

literature.title: Drug–Drug Interactions vs. Therapeutic Combinations in Patients with Congestive Heart Failure and Diabetes: An Ambispective Real‐World Study
literature.what_it_means: Addresses pharmacist medication review workflow and DDI screening, relevant to Waymark's clinical pharmacy program. However, hospitalized setting, small sample, cross-sectional design, and lack of causal inference limit evidence strength. No outcome data on safety or health impact.

literature.title: Target Trial Emulation or Target Trial Approximation?
literature.what_it_means: Directly addresses Waymark's core causal-evaluation method (target-trial emulation). Argues the framework has value but cannot eliminate observational-data limitations. Does not propose new methods or present empirical evidence from Medicaid populations.

literature.title: TrialCalibre1: An Agentic System for Trial Emulation, Benchmarking, and Calibration
literature.what_it_means: TrialCalibre1 addresses Waymark's causal-evaluation interests (target-trial emulation, sensitivity analysis) and AI-safety concerns (protocol review, implementation verification). Preprint; limited validation; design departures and residual imbalance acknowledged.

literature.title: Exploring the impact of GLP-1 analogues and DPP-4 inhibitors on cognitive decline in elderly patients with type 2 diabetes: a competing risks analysis from a real-world cohort
literature.what_it_means: Pharmacist-relevant medication-class comparison in real-world cohort using causal methods (marginal structural models, competing risks). However, study focuses on cognitive outcomes in elderly diabetics—a narrower population than Waymark's broader Medicaid membership. Transfer to Medicaid managed-care pharmacy work requires evidence it improves reach, adherence, or outcomes in Waymark's actual mem

literature.title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes
literature.what_it_means: Novel causal inference method for right-censored survival outcomes under unmeasured confounding. Theoretical contribution with benchmark validation. Medicaid fit unclear; no operational trial or US managed-care setting.

literature.title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
literature.what_it_means: LLM phenotype extraction could support Waymark's clinical NLP work on omission errors and care-note understanding. However, population is pediatric Rett syndrome (rare, specialist-managed), not Medicaid chronic disease or social needs. Transferability unclear.

literature.title: Difference-in-Differences for Heterogeneous Effects of General Treatment Strategies Accounting for Time-Varying Covariates
literature.what_it_means: Waymark explicitly values causal methods for observational data including staggered DiD. This paper directly addresses heterogeneous-effects estimation under time-varying confounding—a core challenge in Waymark's operational context where treatment timing and covariate trajectories vary.

literature.title: SurvICL: a Foundation Model for in-context Survival Analysis
literature.what_it_means: SurvICL could improve risk prediction for whom to reach, but evidence is purely methodological on synthetic/benchmark data, not real clinical cohorts. Medicaid transfer untested. Preprint status.

literature.title: Artificial Intelligence in Health Insurance: An Interagency Framework for Federal and State Oversight
literature.venue: The Journal of law, medicine & ethics : a journal of the American Society of Law, Medicine & Ethics
literature.what_it_means: Policy framework paper on AI governance in insurance, not empirical evidence. Relevant to Waymark's AI deployment and safety concerns, but no data on impact, validation, or operationalization in Medicaid managed care.

literature.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Community Health Worker Interventions for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review
literature.venue: Applied health economics and health policy
literature.what_it_means: Systematic review of CHW cost-effectiveness in T2D is relevant to Waymark's core program. Medicaid fit is transferable but requires caution: studies focused on low-income/minority populations (aligned with Waymark) but global scope and heterogeneous designs limit direct applicability. No US Medicaid-specific evidence synthesis.

literature.title: Prevalent knowledge omissions: An unseen risk of LLMs in patient-friendly adaptation of medical literature
literature.what_it_means: Directly relevant to Waymark's LLM safety concerns (Anchor product, COMPASS). However, uses a dataset of chemical-disease relations, not clinical notes or member-facing text. Transfer to Waymark's actual adaptation workflows requires validation.

literature.title: Dynamic pathways of maternal well-being: A longitudinal latent class analysis of risk and adaptive trajectories in low-income families
literature.what_it_means: Study identifies maternal mental health subgroups and trajectories in low-income populations similar to Waymark's demographic. Findings could inform behavioral health targeting and social needs screening, but lacks intervention component and does not address Medicaid-managed-care care-team workflow.

literature.title: County-Level Context and Differential Policy Impacts on Buprenorphine Use Among Medicaid Enrollees with Opioid Use Disorder in Kentucky, 2018–2025
literature.what_it_means: Interrupted time series of policy changes affecting medication access and use in Medicaid OUD population. Relevant to care coordination outreach and pharmacist medication review, but unclear if findings would inform Waymark's reach, team actions, or product behavior without adaptation.

literature.title: Applications of Transformer-Based pretrained language models for analyzing nursing records in adult Care: A scoping review
literature.what_it_means: Scoping review of NLP methods for unstructured clinical notes. Relevant to Waymark's interest in LLM safety and care-note analysis, but no Medicaid-specific data, no operational validation, and no evidence that these methods improve care or reduce errors in practice.

literature.title: Social Risk Screening and Referrals in the Pediatric Inpatient Setting
literature.what_it_means: Describes screening prevalence and practices but no causal evidence on impact. Inpatient acute setting differs from Waymark's community-based outpatient model. No health outcomes or cost data.

literature.title: Large Language Models in the Emergency Department: Fairness Implications for Clinicians
literature.what_it_means: Addresses LLM fairness risks relevant to Waymark's AI products (Signal, Compass, Anchor). Framework transfers to Medicaid settings but review is narrative, not empirical evidence of specific harms or solutions.

literature.title: Explainable AI in Healthcare: A Holistic View of Technical Approaches, Regulatory Frameworks, Reliable Clinical Implementation Insights and Limitations
literature.what_it_means: Directly relevant to Anchor's verification layer and LLM safety interests. Reviews XAI techniques for bias detection and hallucination reduction—core to Waymark's omission-error evaluation. Limited actionable guidance for Medicaid care-team workflows.

literature.title: Internal Consistency Does Not Validate an LLM-Assisted Nutrition Pipeline: A Reference-Standard-Free Forensic Reliability Audit of 13,073 Free-Text Meal Records
literature.what_it_means: Directly addresses LLM reliability and omission-error detection—core to Waymark's Anchor and Signal products. However, nutrition application in rural Colombia does not transfer to Medicaid care coordination without explicit argument.

literature.title: FERMAT: An Autoregressive Clinical Foundation Model for Disease Risk and Clinical Event Prediction
literature.what_it_means: Foundation model for risk prediction could improve Signal's rising-risk detection, but evidence is from a single hospital's insured population, not Medicaid managed care. No prospective validation or operational deployment shown.

literature.title: Postpartum Medicaid extensions and follow-up care after pregnancy complications
literature.what_it_means: Studies postpartum Medicaid population Waymark serves but focuses narrowly on insurance continuity effect on utilization. Does not directly inform whom to reach, care-team actions, or product behavior without further analysis.

literature.title: Estimation of Area Deprivation Index Rankings in South Dakota Using Spatiotemporal Change of Support Method
literature.what_it_means: Addresses geographic misalignment in SDOH measurement, relevant to targeting. But South Dakota-specific methods paper with no outcomes data, no validation in Medicaid settings, and unclear operational integration.

literature.title: Telepharmacological Consultation for Polypharmacy Management in Primary Care: A Qualitative Study of General Practitioners' Experiences With Cross‐Sectoral Coordination
literature.what_it_means: Qualitative study of pharmacist–GP coordination for polypharmacy in Danish primary care. Addresses pharmacy program workflow integration and care-coordination gaps. Setting differs (single-payer, hospital-based service vs. Medicaid managed care). Small sample limits generalizability.

literature.title: Cognition, oversight, and the safety case for documentation AI
literature.what_it_means: Directly relevant to Anchor's verification layer and LLM-safety interests. Hospital discharge setting differs from Waymark's community-based Medicaid care. Mechanism (oversight attenuation) plausibly transfers; population does not.

literature.title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts
literature.what_it_means: Unreviewed preprint evaluated on 36 EHR benchmark tasks, not members or claims data. It targets temporal and index-date errors that matter given Waymark's claims lag and staggered ADT start dates. It does not show that the resulting effect estimates are valid or survive falsification.

literature.title: Learning Who Benefits Most: Multi-Treatment Causal Ranking for Population Health Stratification
literature.what_it_means: Unreviewed preprint tested only on synthetic and semi-synthetic data from the Italian system. Waymark's per-member treatment-effect rankings did not validate out of sample, and recovering generated orderings does not address that failure. Revisit if a real-outcome validation appears.

literature.title: Seeded Probes Do Not Identify a Reviewer's Miss Rate: One-Sided Misclassification in Distribution-Free Risk Control
literature.what_it_means: Anchor and Compass safety rest on physician review of AI outputs. The paper argues that planted-error probes cannot validate those reviewers. Physician miss rates varied widely. The argument is mainly formal and fits any setting, but this is an unreviewed preprint with simulations and a small empirical sample of 17 physicians.

literature.title: Adjudicator sensitivity of safety estimates in large language models for open-ended cardiovascular reasoning: a blinded multi-adjudicator benchmark study running title: adjudicator variability in LLM safety
literature.what_it_means: This is a peer-reviewed methods study. One adjudicator flagged 17.7% of responses as unsafe and the other flagged 0%. Single-reviewer safety audits like this bear directly on how Waymark validates Anchor and Compass outputs. The domain is cardiology, not Medicaid, but the measurement problem transfers.

literature.title: A Machine Learning Approach to Linking Medicaid and Education Records in New York City
literature.venue: International Journal for Population Data Science
literature.what_it_means: Peer-reviewed methods work on Medicaid children's records. It is relevant to linking messy administrative sources such as claims, ADT and CBO referral data. It does not change whom Waymark reaches or what teams do. Education linkage is not a current Waymark data source. Linkage accuracy is reported only as a match rate, with no outcomes.

literature.title: Factors Associated with Early ED Return Among Patients Discharged After Treatment for Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome
literature.what_it_means: Single-site retrospective review with only 14 72-hour returns. Covariates were picked by univariate screening, and the confidence intervals are very wide. The risk factors it finds (serious mental illness, homelessness) are already expected. It is relevant to post-ED outreach for alcohol withdrawal, but too fragile to change targeting or care-team actions.

literature.title: “I don't have to choose between everything”: Self-reported fruit and vegetable affordability, purchasing shifts, and healthcare utilization among produce prescription program participants in North Carolina
literature.what_it_means: Low-income food-insecure population is relevant to Medicaid social-needs work, but the evidence is weak: an uncontrolled online survey with recalled before/after affordability. The causal conclusions about improved affordability and healthcare use are not supported by this design. No claims-based outcomes. Worth tracking alongside controlled produce-prescription evaluations.

literature.title: Assessing the ability of cross-trained pharmacy technician-community health workers to identify non-medical drivers of health resources
literature.venue: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA
literature.what_it_means: Descriptive analysis of training assignments, not patient encounters. It reports no referral completion, no member outcomes and no Medicaid-specific population. Cross-training pharmacy staff as CHWs is conceptually relevant to Waymark's team mix, but nothing here would change practice or evaluation yet.

literature.title: Embedded Psychological Services and Lower 60-Day Acute-Care Utilization in High-Need, High-Cost Adults: A Target Trial Emulation
literature.venue: The journal of behavioral health services & research
literature.what_it_means: The population closely resembles Waymark's members. But comparing engagers with decliners and no-shows invites healthy-adherer bias, which weighting on measured confounders cannot remove. An E-value of 2.37 is plausible for motivation. Admissions were null. This conflicts with Waymark's lesson favoring quasi-random operational variation.

literature.title: A University and Community Partnership to Address Diaper Insecurity Among Infants in Suburban Communities Through Home Visiting Services
literature.venue: Journal of public health management and practice : JPHMP
literature.what_it_means: The population and the CHW home-visit model closely match Waymark's pediatric Medicaid work. But this is a descriptive, post-only survey of 88 respondents with self-reported outcomes and no comparison group. It shows feasibility, not effect, so it is not enough to change practice yet.

literature.title: Federal Immigration Enforcement Deployment and Emergency Department Utilization Among Children
literature.what_it_means: The urban pediatric safety-net population likely overlaps heavily with Medicaid, and VA is nearby. But this is one site over a short window, the unit is visits not children, and outcomes are unlinked, so care avoidance cannot be told apart from shifts to other sites. It points to equity and evaluation risk, not a validated intervention.

literature.title: Patient Navigation Plus mHealth Incentives for Linkage to OUD Care for Adults Who Also Use Methamphetamines
literature.what_it_means: Small single-site pilot RCT at a Washington safety-net hospital, a population close to Waymark's. Linkage was 55% vs 50%, with a wide CI around a risk ratio of 1.10, so effectiveness is unknown. Feasibility and acceptability of navigation are encouraging, but it is not enough to change practice yet.

literature.title: Protocol for the Nutrition OUtReach In Systems of Healthcare (NOURISH) trial: a phase II multicentre, parallel-group randomised controlled trial of medically tailored groceries to prevent malnutrition in transplant and cellular therapy patients
literature.what_it_means: It reports no outcomes. The population is a narrow, high-acuity oncology transplant group in specialty centers, and payer mix is unreported. The planned sample is modest, and the primary endpoint is clinical malnutrition rather than utilization. Results could still inform food-as-medicine referral design.

literature.title: Low‐Intensity Social Care for Dementia Caregivers: A Randomized Trial
literature.venue: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
literature.what_it_means: Peer-reviewed RCT with a null primary outcome. The ED reduction is a secondary, self-reported finding with a wide CI from a small sample. The population (low-income, mostly Black, US urban) plausibly transfers, but it was not Medicaid-specific. Text-navigator uptake was high.

literature.title: Impact of a National Stepped‐Care Model of Opioid Use Disorder Treatment on Access to Medication Therapies Among Homeless‐Experienced Veterans
literature.what_it_means: Facility-level train-the-trainer support for stepped-care opioid use disorder treatment in non-specialty settings was associated with higher buprenorphine receipt among homeless patients with opioid use disorder, with no change in methadone or naltrexone.

literature.title: Self-Adjusting Long-Term Medications: A Qualitative Descriptive Study of Patients’ Practices
literature.what_it_means: Small descriptive interview study. Country, payer and patient characteristics are not reported, so transfer to Medicaid members is unclear. It describes reasons for self-adjustment but tests no intervention. The themes may inform how pharmacists frame medication reviews, but it is not enough to change practice.

literature.title: Woebot for Postpartum Mood and Anxiety: Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating Feasibility, Acceptability, and Preliminary Efficacy of a Mobile Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Intervention
literature.what_it_means: Pilot RCT with a waitlist control and self-reported outcomes. The efficacy signal is weak (d=-0.16, n=97 symptomatic), and the improvement in stress was exploratory. The sample was mostly White, recruited through a research platform, and payer was not reported, so the Medicaid postpartum transfer is unproven. Engagement was modest, a median of 9 days.

literature.title: Personalizing digital mental health: a micro-randomized trial analysis of cognitive behavioral therapy/dialectical behavioral therapy text messages to improve mood
literature.what_it_means: The design is relevant to Compass message timing, but average effects were null. The moderator findings come from multiple subgroup tests and were not replicated. The sample was mostly highly educated White women from social media, not Medicaid members. Waymark's own heterogeneous-effect rankings failed to validate out of sample.

literature.title: Outpatient Antibiotic Fills and 30-Day Readmission Following Patient-Directed Discharge in Drug Use-Associated Infective Endocarditis in a National Medicaid Cohort
literature.venue: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
literature.what_it_means: This is a direct Medicaid population with a clear high-risk, reachable subgroup: patients who leave against medical advice. The low fill rate is a robust descriptive target. The protective link between antibiotic fill and readmission is observational and likely confounded by healthy-adherer bias, so it does not prove that outreach would cut readmissions.

literature.title: Use of digital health tools to promote equitable and efficient health-related social needs screening and response
literature.venue: Current problems in pediatric and adolescent health care
literature.what_it_means: This is a narrative review with no new data, no comparison and no outcome estimates. The topic matches Waymark's social-needs screening and SMS navigation work. Its trauma-informed privacy framing may help with design, but it provides no evidence that would change practice or product behavior.

literature.title: Skill-guided agentic reasoning enables longitudinal synthesis of myeloma records at expert-level concordance
literature.what_it_means: The core result is a specialty-oncology benchmark, not a Medicaid population. The safety finding is relevant to Anchor: comparable error rates can hide a higher share of clinically significant errors. Skill libraries also helped plain retrieval-augmented generation. The study is retrospective and single-domain, with no evidence on patient outcomes.

literature.title: Feasibility of Implementing a Pharmacist-Integrated Collaborative Model for Opioid Use Disorder: A Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
literature.what_it_means: A single-arm pre-post feasibility study at four sites with no control and no significance testing. The adherence and retention changes are tiny and noisy, and the total sample size isn't reported. MOUD patients are heavily Medicaid, so the topic is relevant, but the study shows feasibility, not effectiveness.

published_findings.title: Comparing Alternative Approaches to Care Management Prioritization: A Prospective Comparative Cohort Study of Acute Care Utilization and Equity Among Medicaid Beneficiaries
published_findings.headline: Targeting care management by predicted benefit beats targeting by risk
published_findings.finding: Prioritizing Medicaid outreach by predicted benefit, rather than predicted risk, was associated with 92 fewer acute care visits per thousand member-months, with similar engagement rates.
published_findings.why_surprising: Conventional wisdom targets the sickest or highest-risk patients for intensive care management. This study shows that identifying patients most likely to benefit from intervention—regardless of baseline risk—achieves better results with the same engagement effort.

published_findings.title: Treatment-Effect-Based Versus Risk-Based Targeting of Care Management Outreach in Medicaid: A Retrospective Cohort Study with Machine Learning
published_findings.headline: Targeting by predicted treatment effect prevents about 5x more acute events
published_findings.finding: At the same outreach capacity, allocating care-management calls by predicted treatment effect was estimated to prevent 5.3 times as many acute events as allocating by risk (95% CI 4.9 to 5.7), without widening group disparities.
published_findings.why_surprising: Care-management programs conventionally target high-risk patients, assuming those at greatest risk benefit most. This study found that patients most likely to benefit from outreach differ markedly from those at highest risk, and that matching individuals to outreach based on responsiveness rather than risk yielded substantially better outcomes.

published_findings.title: Preventing tomorrow's high-cost claims: the rising-risk patient opportunity in Medicaid
published_findings.venue: The American journal of managed care
published_findings.headline: Targeting rising-risk patients beats focusing on current high-cost claimants
published_findings.finding: Spending for rising-risk Medicaid patients nearly doubled over the year while spending for high-cost claimants fell 41.6% as costs regressed to the mean; half of new high-cost claimants had been flagged as rising risk.
published_findings.why_surprising: Standard practice targets current high-cost claimants for intervention. This analysis shows high-cost status is often temporary due to regression to the mean, while rising-risk patients represent the true cost trajectory. Early intervention on rising-risk patients addresses disease progression before it peaks.

published_findings.title: The Risk Of Perpetuating Health Disparities Through Cost-Effectiveness Analyses
published_findings.headline: Cost-effectiveness analyses may systematically disadvantage minority groups
published_findings.finding: Standard cost-effectiveness approaches can make interventions for marginalized groups appear less cost-effective than for advantaged groups by incorporating assumptions that perpetuate existing health inequities, such as differences in baseline costs and competing risks.
published_findings.why_surprising: Cost-effectiveness analysis is intended as a neutral policy tool. Yet standard methods embed structural inequities—like baseline health care costs and insurance status—that make interventions targeting disadvantaged populations look worse on paper, even when addressing greater health needs.

published_findings.title: Clinical decision support for population health management: development and validation of integrated acuity and intervention prediction models
published_findings.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
published_findings.headline: Integrated decision support flags acute care risk before it shows up in claims
published_findings.finding: Integrated prediction model achieved 81.3% sensitivity and 82.1% specificity for 30-day acute care prediction, with 1.59 percentage point absolute risk reduction compared with standard care.
published_findings.why_surprising: Physicians typically make sound clinical decisions, but they relied heavily on recent utilization patterns (75.8% of variance) while models integrated broader signals to identify intervention needs earlier. The modest but consistent risk reduction shows models complement rather than replace clinical judgment.

published_findings.title: Prediction of non emergent acute care utilization and cost among patients receiving Medicaid
published_findings.headline: Better data triples detection of high-risk Medicaid patients and corrects racial bias
published_findings.finding: Adding richer data tripled sensitivity for at-risk patients (11.3% vs 3.4%) at near-identical specificity and reversed the standard cost-based model's lower sensitivity for Black versus White patients.
published_findings.why_surprising: Risk models for Medicaid patients have historically performed poorly due to incomplete data. This confirms that collecting better social risk data substantially improves their ability to find high-risk patients—a meaningful validation of this common-sense approach.

published_findings.title: Medicare Advantage and Type 2 Diabetes Outcomes
published_findings.headline: Medicare Advantage not linked to better diabetes outcomes than original Medicare
published_findings.finding: Among adults with type 2 diabetes, Medicare Advantage was not associated with better hemoglobin A1c, blood pressure, cholesterol, food insecurity, housing instability, or transportation barriers compared with original Medicare.
published_findings.why_surprising: Medicare Advantage plans market financial protections and supplemental benefits (food assistance, transportation) specifically designed to address social needs and improve diabetes outcomes. One might expect these additional benefits to produce measurable health gains, but the study finds no difference in any clinical or social outcome.

published_findings.title: Opportunistic Cardiovascular Risk Assessment Using Routine Head CT in the Emergency Department
published_findings.venue: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
published_findings.headline: Routine emergency head CT scans reveal hidden cardiovascular risk
published_findings.finding: Deep learning on routine emergency head CT scans added to traditional risk factors for predicting cardiovascular events, flagging subclinical disease in younger patients with favorable risk profiles.
published_findings.why_surprising: Head CT is ordered for neurological reasons, not cardiac risk assessment. Most clinicians would expect cardiac-specific imaging or biomarkers to outperform incidental findings. This shows routine scans contain useful cardiovascular information and identified younger patients with subclinical disease that traditional models missed.

published_findings.title: Transferring healthcare risk prediction models between Medicaid populations: a transfer learning evaluation
published_findings.headline: Simple model transfer matches complex methods for predicting acute care use
published_findings.finding: A basic transfer approach achieved similar discrimination as a sophisticated meta-ensemble when predicting acute care utilization across Medicaid populations, with recalibration substantially improving calibration.
published_findings.why_surprising: Complex transfer learning methods like domain-adversarial networks and Enhanced MAML are often expected to outperform naive approaches when adapting models across populations with different demographics and outcome prevalence. This finding shows simpler solutions work equally well.

published_findings.title: Early detection of high risk pregnancies using clinical and social data to improve health outcomes
published_findings.headline: Adding social data to pregnancy risk models boosts sensitivity by 10 points
published_findings.finding: Adding social data, especially health care access, raised sensitivity for high-risk pregnancies from 71.3% to 81.3% at 94.3% specificity and narrowed the gap between Black and White patients.
published_findings.why_surprising: While social determinants' link to maternal outcomes is known, most clinical risk models rely primarily on medical history. This shows that systematically incorporating SDoH data meaningfully improves prediction accuracy and, notably, reduces algorithmic bias—a practical validation of equity benefits often discussed theoretically.

published_findings.title: Offline reinforcement learning for care management: addressing sparse rewards, temporal dependencies, and fairness in Medicaid populations
published_findings.headline: Doubly robust evaluation stabilizes reinforcement learning for Medicaid care decisions
published_findings.finding: Standard off-policy evaluation achieved 0% effective sample size due to variance inflation, while doubly robust evaluation achieved 44.2%, enabling stable policy assessment. Fairness constraints reduced racial/ethnic intervention disparities from 3.5 to 0.8 percentage points.
published_findings.why_surprising: High-dimensional action spaces typically cause extreme variance in off-policy evaluation, making policy assessment unreliable. This result demonstrates that doubly robust methods can achieve stability, and that fairness constraints simultaneously reduce disparities—a combination not often demonstrated together.

published_findings.title: Redesigning Medicaid frailty algorithms: improved identification of medically frail adults under community engagement
published_findings.headline: Redesigned frailty algorithm identifies 45% more disabled Medicaid adults
published_findings.finding: Existing state algorithms identified mean 31.4% of functionally disabled Medicaid adults as medically frail. A redesigned algorithm incorporating expanded diagnostics increased identification to 45.6%, narrowing racial disparities by 10-46%.
published_findings.why_surprising: States use widely varying thresholds for frailty exemptions despite serving similar populations. A standardized, evidence-based approach substantially improves identification across all states and reduces racial and rural-urban gaps.

published_findings.title: Integrating healthcare system context to improve risk prediction and assess racial disparities among dual-eligible Medicare-Medicaid beneficiaries: a retrospective cohort study using national fee-for-service claims
published_findings.headline: System context reshapes spending risk differently by race
published_findings.finding: Adding healthcare system context to risk models reduced predicted spending for 86% of dual-eligible beneficiaries (mean 8.8 percentage points), but increased it for 14%. Black beneficiaries experienced higher contextual risk amplification (15.8% vs 13.6% White).
published_findings.why_surprising: Risk models typically focus on individual health factors. This finds that system-level factors like care coordination and workforce substantially reshape predictions—and reveals these factors affect racial groups differently, suggesting current models may mask important disparities.

published_findings.title: Medicaid Managed Care Procurement Reveals Systematic Overemphasis of Technology and Equity Performance Claims Across 32 States
published_findings.venue: Inquiry : a journal of medical care organization, provision and financing
published_findings.headline: Medicaid insurers overemphasize trendy topics in contracts, downplay chronic disease care
published_findings.finding: Managed care organizations made 54 times more technology claims and 22 times more health equity claims than state requirements, while underemphasizing chronic disease management and workforce development.
published_findings.why_surprising: You might expect insurance companies to focus contract promises on areas states explicitly require. Instead, they systematically emphasize politically popular topics like technology and equity while de-emphasizing unglamorous but essential services like managing diabetes. This reveals a gap between what sounds good and what actually improves care.

published_findings.title: AI safety evaluation in an underrepresented population: real-world performance of clinical decision support and frontier language models on Medicaid patient messaging triage
published_findings.venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
published_findings.headline: AI triage tools need physician oversight for Medicaid patient safety
published_findings.finding: No AI tool or combination achieved both 0.80 sensitivity and specificity for autonomous triage. Best balanced ensemble reached 0.69 sensitivity and 0.58 specificity; highest specificity had only 0.30 sensitivity.
published_findings.why_surprising: Frontier language models and ensemble approaches often outperform individual tools on benchmarks. Real-world Medicaid messages with lower reading levels and colloquialisms revealed that even sophisticated AI combinations cannot reliably identify clinical hazards without physician review, suggesting benchmarks overstate real-world safety.

published_findings.title: Association of Multidisciplinary Care Team Engagement With Hemoglobin A1c Among Medicaid Enrollees With Diabetes: A Doubly Robust Machine Learning Analysis
published_findings.headline: Diabetes care teams help most patients with worst control
published_findings.finding: Multidisciplinary care team engagement associated with 0.30 percentage point A1c reduction. Benefit increased per unit higher baseline A1c; among those with baseline A1c ≥9%, reduction approached 1 percentage point.
published_findings.why_surprising: The overall effect is modest, which might seem disappointing. However, benefits concentrate sharply among people with the worst baseline control (≥9% A1c), differing from typical interventions that show more uniform effects. This supports targeting resources to sickest patients.

published_findings.title: Quantifying Indirect Billing Within the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule
published_findings.headline: About 39% of clinician office visits are billed under physicians' names
published_findings.finding: Advanced practice clinicians provided a substantial share of Medicare office visits, and 38.9% of their office encounters were billed indirectly under physicians, hiding who delivers the care.
published_findings.why_surprising: While indirect billing is permitted under Medicare rules, the magnitude is notable: APCs provide substantial care yet bill under physician names at rates varying widely by specialty (about 30% in surgery vs. 4% in primary care), suggesting billing patterns may reflect business practices more than clinical necessity.

published_findings.title: Procedural Prescription Denials and Risk of Acute Care Utilization and Spending Among Medicaid Patients
published_findings.headline: Some prescription denials cost Medicaid more than they save
published_findings.finding: Some procedural prescription denials were associated with more emergency visits and hospital stays, with acute care costs that outweighed the short-term drug savings.
published_findings.why_surprising: Health plans deny prescriptions to reduce drug costs, but this study shows the approach backfires for some medication classes. The acute care utilization from untreated chronic conditions outweighs initial savings, resulting in net cost increases.

published_findings.title: Prevalence and Geographic Variation of Serious Mental Illness Among Young Adults Enrolled in Medicaid in New York State
published_findings.venue: The Journal of adolescent health : official publication of the Society for Adolescent Medicine
published_findings.headline: Homelessness carries the highest odds of serious mental illness in young adults
published_findings.finding: Among young adults enrolled in Medicaid, homelessness (odds ratio 5.49), disability, female sex and rural residence were associated with higher odds of serious mental illness.
published_findings.why_surprising: Racial and ethnic minorities typically face greater barriers to mental health care and higher social stressors, so we'd expect higher SMI rates. This finding suggests either protective factors in these communities, differences in diagnosis/treatment-seeking, or measurement issues that differ by race.

published_findings.title: Predicting quality measure completion among 14 million low-income patients enrolled in medicaid
published_findings.headline: Clinical data alone predicts Medicaid quality gaps better than random outreach
published_findings.finding: A model using clinical data improved accuracy by 32.5 percentage points over non-predictive methods like alphabetical calling. Adding social determinants data improved accuracy to 84.5% and reduced racial disparities in predictions.
published_findings.why_surprising: Most outreach to low-income patients uses simple methods like birthday reminders or alphabetical calling. This shows that even basic predictive models dramatically outperform these approaches, and that social data further narrows racial prediction gaps—an outcome targeting typically fails to achieve.

published_findings.title: Medicaid Expansion Among Nonelderly Adults and Cardiovascular Disease: Efficiency Vs. Equity
published_findings.headline: Medicaid expansion associated with fewer heart attacks and strokes
published_findings.finding: Medicaid expansion was associated with fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths among nonelderly adults, with the largest gains for lower-income, Black and Hispanic adults; the estimates are uncertain.
published_findings.why_surprising: Common concerns about Medicaid focus on program costs rather than health gains. This shows expansion redistributed health gains toward lower-income groups, though cost-effectiveness remained uncertain (only 26–29% confidence it was both efficient and equity-enhancing).

published_findings.title: Reinforcement Learning to Prevent Acute Care Events Among Medicaid Populations: Mixed Methods Study
published_findings.headline: Reinforcement-learning-guided care management linked to fewer acute events
published_findings.finding: Care management guided by a reinforcement-learning policy was associated with a 20.7% relative reduction in acute care events compared with standard practice (number needed to treat 8.3).
published_findings.why_surprising: Care managers rely on experience and judgment to prioritize interventions. This result shows an algorithmic approach trained on patient trajectories can identify better intervention sequences than experienced practitioners, and does so more fairly across demographic groups.

published_findings.title: Simulating A/B testing versus SMART designs for LLM-driven patient engagement to close preventive care gaps
published_findings.headline: SMART design outperforms A/B testing for tailoring patient engagement messages
published_findings.finding: In simulations comparing designs for testing personalized outreach, SMART showed better cost-effectiveness and net benefit across all scenarios, with superior power for detecting heterogeneous treatment effects in later stages.
published_findings.why_surprising: A/B testing is the standard approach for message testing in health programs. SMART's advantage here may surprise because it's less familiar and requires more complex implementation, yet simulation shows it delivers better results while being more cost-effective.

published_findings.title: Preferences for food vouchers among adults with low incomes
published_findings.headline: Low-income adults prefer unrestricted food vouchers over produce-only options
published_findings.finding: Participants preferred vouchers eligible for all foods over fruit and vegetable restrictions, and monthly over weekly redemption schedules. Preferences shifted based on actual voucher assignment.
published_findings.why_surprising: Health programs typically restrict vouchers to nutrient-dense foods to maximize health benefit. This finding shows participants value flexibility and convenience over program design intended to guide healthier choices, though preferences adapted to their assigned voucher type.

published_findings.title: Impact of Vietnam-era G.I. Bill eligibility on later-life blood pressure distribution: evidence from the Vietnam draft lottery natural experiment
published_findings.headline: G.I. Bill eligibility lowered later-life blood pressure, most for poorer men
published_findings.finding: Vietnam-era G.I. Bill eligibility shifted the blood pressure distribution toward lower risk, with a 3 mmHg lower systolic pressure at the 90th percentile and benefits concentrated in men from lower-income childhoods.
published_findings.why_surprising: Education subsidies target academic opportunity, not health directly. That college eligibility specifically benefits blood pressure distribution at higher quantiles—reducing concentrated morbidity risk—rather than uniformly across all pressure levels adds nuance to how early-life opportunity shapes adult cardiovascular health.

published_findings.title: Comparison of Self and Caregiver Reports of Antiretroviral Treatment Adherence among Children and Adolescents Living with HIV in Western Kenya
published_findings.venue: Journal of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care
published_findings.headline: Child and caregiver reports of HIV medication adherence equally inaccurate
published_findings.finding: Child and caregiver self-reports were similarly associated with objective pill bottle data (correlations 0.23 and 0.20), and both groups under-reported missed doses compared to actual adherence measured by pill bottle caps.
published_findings.why_surprising: One might expect caregivers to have better visibility into adherence patterns, making their reports more accurate. This study found child and caregiver reports were equally unreliable compared to objective measurement, suggesting similar blind spots in both perspectives.

published_findings.title: Association of Adequacy of Broadband Internet Service With Access to Primary Care in the Veterans Health Administration Before and During the COVID-19 Pandemic
published_findings.headline: Better broadband access associated with more virtual primary care visits
published_findings.finding: Veterans with optimal broadband had more video primary care visits and fewer in-person visits after the pandemic began than those with inadequate broadband.
published_findings.why_surprising: One might expect broadband access to simply enable telemedicine as an additional option without reducing in-person care. This shows that better broadband availability was associated with a meaningful shift away from in-person visits, raising questions about whether virtual care fully substitutes for or complements in-person primary care.

published_findings.title: Catastrophic Spending On Insulin In The United States, 2017-18
published_findings.headline: One in seven insulin users face catastrophic out-of-pocket costs
published_findings.finding: Among Americans using insulin, 14.1% spent more than 40% of postsubsistence family income on insulin annually. Catastrophic spending was 61% less likely among Medicaid than Medicare beneficiaries.
published_findings.why_surprising: Medicare covers seniors and disabled people, typically lower-income groups. One might expect better protection than Medicaid, yet Medicare beneficiaries face higher catastrophic spending. This suggests insurance design, not just income, drives vulnerability.

published_findings.title: The Underuse of Medicare's Prevention and Coordination Codes in Primary Care : A Cross-Sectional and Modeling Study
published_findings.headline: Primary care doctors bill for prevention services to only 2% of eligible patients
published_findings.finding: Median billing code use was 2.3% among eligible patients, even though doctors provided appropriate services to 5-61% of eligible patients. If doctors billed half of eligible patients, annual revenue could increase by $124k for prevention and $86k for coordination services.
published_findings.why_surprising: One might expect that if Medicare added billing codes to support primary care, doctors would readily use them to capture available revenue. Instead, most forgo substantial annual income—potentially over $200k per practice—by not billing for services they already provide, suggesting barriers beyond code availability.

published_findings.title: How the Gender Wage Gap for Primary Care Physicians Differs by Compensation Approach : A Microsimulation Study
published_findings.headline: Risk-adjusting pay for patient age and sex narrows primary care physician gender wage gap
published_findings.finding: Female PCPs earned 21% less than male PCPs under productivity-based pay. The gap narrowed to a nonsignificant difference under capitation risk-adjusted for patient age and sex, compared to larger gaps under other risk-adjustment approaches.
published_findings.why_surprising: Female PCPs see younger, healthier, and more Medicaid-insured patients—factors that reduce revenue under most payment models. Counterintuitively, accounting for patient sex in risk adjustment (along with age) substantially closes the gap, suggesting common risk models miss a key driver of compensation differences.
